KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Wang
Saffron Park Hospital

Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL
Dear Dr Wang
Alex Carter, DOB: 14-05-2006, Hospital No: P903772 NHS No. 7712390045
Flat 3, 12 Kingsbridge Lane, London, E14 6PA 

I reviewed the above patient in the Adult Neurology Clinic today following transition from paediatric services. A parent attended and contributed helpful collateral history. He has a confirmed diagnosis of generalised epilepsy.

This is our first adult clinic review post-transition. From the joint handover summary and today’s history, his typical episodes comprise brief staring spells with eyelid flutter and occasional myoclonic jerks shortly after waking. Generalised tonic–clonic seizures have been infrequent. At present he reports clusters of brief absence episodes every 4 weeks, usually over 1–2 days, often precipitated by reduced sleep and academic stress. His last generalised tonic–clonic seizure was in May 2025 after a night of sleep deprivation, and there have been none since.

He is taking Sodium Valproate 500 mg b.d. and Levetiracetam (Keppra) 1 g b.d. with good adherence. He describes mild morning lethargy and intermittent low mood around examination periods, which he and his parent feel are manageable. No rashes, visual disturbance, or focal neurological symptoms were reported. There is no history of focal onset phenomena. He is not driving.

On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal speech and language. Cranial nerves were intact, tone and power were normal in all limbs, reflexes were symmetric, and coordination and gait were normal. There were no neurocutaneous stigmata.

Paediatric EEGs have shown generalised spike–wave discharges, most recently in 2024. MRI brain (2023) was normal. We will arrange an updated EEG to reassess background and interictal activity in the adult service and to support ongoing management planning. Given his current pattern of absence clusters every 4 weeks without recent convulsions, I have not altered medication today. We discussed adherence, regular sleep, and stress management as practical measures that may help reduce breakthrough events. He and his parent were given information on our transition nurse specialist and epilepsy advisor should they wish to discuss education or lifestyle issues further.

I have asked him to keep a simple seizure diary, noting any absence clusters and possible triggers, particularly sleep loss. We will review him in 6 months, or sooner if events increase in frequency, if he experiences any adverse effects, or if a generalised tonic–clonic seizure recurs.

Yours sincerely

Department of Neurology

Clinic Date: 15 January 2014

Dr A. Rahman
Southbank Neurology Clinic
Level 3, Riverside Health Centre, 12 Thames Walk, London SE1 7AB

Dear Dr A. Rahman,

Mr Amir Khan, DOB: 14-03-1992, Hospital No: H394572 NHS No. 1093847562
Flat 2, 15 Brook Street, London W1K 4EA

Diagnoses:

Focal epilepsy with impaired awareness; MRI brain unremarkable (reported last month). Routine EEG pending.

Current Medication:

Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily

Plan:

- Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily while we complete diagnostic work-up
- Arrange routine EEG and consider prolonged ambulatory EEG depending on results
- Provide written seizure first-aid advice and signpost to local epilepsy charity and NHS resources
- Follow up in 6 weeks with interpreter support as needed

I reviewed Mr Amir Khan in clinic today. They are a recent migrant to the UK and are still learning how to access NHS pathways; they sometimes attend with interpreter support and requested written information in plain English. They describe brief episodes starting with a rising epigastric sensation and déjà vu, followed by staring and loss of awareness for 1–2 minutes, with tiredness afterwards. These events have been occurring multiple times in past week, including two episodes witnessed by a friend. There have been no generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported.

The semiology and progression are most consistent with focal epilepsy. We discussed common triggers (sleep deprivation, missed doses, stress). Mr Amir Khan reports good adherence to levetiracetam since initiation overseas three months ago, without mood changes or rash. Safety advice was reviewed, including temporary avoidance of hazardous heights, swimming alone, and cooking over open flames during periods of frequent events. They do not currently drive; we discussed that UK driving regulations require notification to the DVLA for people with epilepsy.

We will obtain a routine EEG locally and, if inconclusive, consider ambulatory monitoring to capture habitual events. MRI brain performed abroad was reportedly normal; images have been uploaded and a local neuroradiology review is requested. Blood tests for antiseizure medication levels are not indicated for levetiracetam, but baseline FBC/U&E/LFTs have been ordered today.

We provided written signposting to NHS resources and local community support, including options for interpreter-assisted appointments. A follow-up appointment is arranged for six weeks to review EEG results, seizure diary entries, and consider optimisation of therapy if events persist.

With best wishes,

Generalised epilepsy with prior EEG demonstrating generalised spike-and-wave activity (2017)

Levetiracetam 1 g bd

- Optimise sleep hygiene around long-haul travel; structured jet‑lag plan provided

I reviewed Michael Turner via scheduled telephone appointment today, consistent with his frequent business travel pattern across multiple time zones. He reports irregular sleep, prolonged flights, and variable meal schedules, often with overnight work calls. Over the last four weeks he has experienced many convulsions in past month, described as sudden loss of awareness followed by generalised tonic–clonic activity lasting 1–2 minutes with tongue‑bite on one occasion and post‑ictal confusion for up to an hour. We discussed practical measures tailored to his travel: bringing a medication schedule card aligned to destination time, setting dual‑time alarms, avoiding red‑eye flights where feasible, and prioritising the first two nights of consolidated sleep. I advised he keeps a rescue plan; clobazam has been helpful around long‑haul trips and can be used cautiously for anticipated sleep deprivation. I also provided written seizure first‑aid for colleagues.

In summary, breakthrough seizures have coincided with disrupted sleep and rapid time‑zone changes; there have been many convulsions in past month. The plan focuses on optimising circadian alignment and dosing timing, with close follow‑up by phone.

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, Denmark Hill, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Harris, DOB: 14-03-1989, Hospital No: KCH-782311 NHS No. 9432015876  
12 Brookside Close, London, SE15 3QT

Thank you for your referral. I reviewed Daniel Harris following concerns raised by his employer about recurrent collapse events occurring during shifts in a commercial kitchen. He works the hot line in a high-temperature, fast-paced environment, often during evening service. He attended today with his colleague who has witnessed several recent episodes.

According to the colleague, the typical event begins without warning while he is plating or working over the grill. He becomes unresponsive, stares ahead, and his posture slackens; there may be low, indistinct vocal sounds. On two occasions he slid down a stainless-steel unit and briefly rocked at the shoulders. There has been no clearly observed rhythmic limb jerking, tongue biting, or incontinence reported. He appears confused after the episode and needs 30–60 minutes before he can resume tasks, often describing a heavy head and overwhelming fatigue. He does not reliably recall the event itself.

Daniel Harris reports that these episodes crop up most shifts, especially during the busiest part of service, and his manager has had to reassign him from open flame stations as a precaution. He also notes that, on getting home, he sometimes wakes disoriented on the sofa with no memory of lying down, suggesting possible unwitnessed events outside work as well. Heat, noise, and pressure to keep pace may be contributory triggers from his perspective.

Medication history: he has recently restarted levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily after a lapse in adherence due to rota changes and missed GP appointments; he believes that when he takes treatment consistently, the kitchen events thin out to only the odd occurrence across a handful of shifts. He denies alcohol misuse; he drinks coffee during service and little fluid otherwise. Sleep is fragmented due to alternating late finishes and early prep starts.

Examination today was unremarkable. Neurological assessment between episodes showed normal cranial nerves, full strength, intact coordination, and no focal deficits. Cardiovascular observations were stable with no orthostatic drop. There were no features to suggest an active intercurrent illness. Collateral descriptions are limited by the hectic nature of the kitchen and the lack of continuous observation.

Given the ongoing events arising on most working days and the safety-critical environment (sharp tools, hot oil, open flames), further characterisation is necessary. I have requested urgent ambulatory EEG with concurrent event diary, and I will also arrange a sleep-deprived EEG if the first study is non-diagnostic. Basic bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, glucose, magnesium) and serum antiseizure medication level have been ordered. I have advised the employer and patient that a temporary restriction from high-risk stations is prudent pending assessment, and the patient will discuss adjusted duties with occupational health. We also talked about hydration and structured meal breaks during service, as he reports going long stretches without fluids.

Daniel Harris understands the plan and agrees to keep a detailed log of events, noting timing, context (heat level, task, stress), and recovery period. I will review him in clinic after investigations. Please let me know if there is any additional history from primary care that would assist, particularly previous imaging or prior EEG results.

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Ahmed  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Sophie Williams, DOB: 23-04-1991, Hospital No: H583920 NHS No. 9842157306  
12 Briar Close, London, W10 5QP 

Medication: 

Valproate (Epilim) 500 mg morning / 1000 mg evening. Levetiracetam (Keppra) 750 mg twice daily. 

I reviewed Sophie Williams in clinic today. She has generalised epilepsy with typical absence episodes and occasional generalised tonic–clonic seizures. Over the past two months she reports brief absences occurring on most weekdays, often clustering around late afternoon when she is more tired. There has been one generalised tonic–clonic seizure in the last eight weeks, witnessed at home. 

Her primary carer accompanied her and notes that increased fatigue has been noticeable since the levetiracetam dose was optimised three months ago. The carer also reports that the patient’s caregiving responsibilities at home (supporting an elderly relative with mobility needs) have led to shortened sleep and irregular mealtimes, which may be lowering her threshold for breakthrough events. The patient describes the tiredness as "heavy" by early evening and finds concentration dips during routine tasks. No new focal features, no injuries, and recovery is prompt after the briefer events. 

On current therapy, tolerability is otherwise acceptable: no mood instability beyond mild irritability late in the day, no gastrointestinal upset, and weight stable. She is using a pill organiser and has not missed doses to her knowledge. There is no reported alcohol use and caffeine is modest. Menses are regular and not clearly linked to a change in seizure pattern. 

Given the frequency pattern—most weekdays for brief absences with infrequent generalised convulsions—we discussed strategies to address fatigue and reduce triggers in the caregiving context. The patient and carer prefer to maintain the present antiepileptic regimen for now and focus on sleep regularity and planned respite support. I have not changed medication today. We agreed the following: 

- Carer to coordinate short daily rest periods for the patient, aiming for a consistent sleep window and a brief early afternoon break.  
- Hydration and regular meals to reduce late-day dips that appear to precede absences.  
- Seizure diary to log timing in relation to sleep debt and caregiving tasks, to guide any future dose adjustments.  

Safety and driving were reviewed in accordance with DVLA guidance for generalised epilepsy. The patient is aware of the need to avoid bath bathing unsupervised and to take extra care with cooking when overtired. We also discussed community support options; the carer will contact the local carers’ centre regarding respite. 

If the weekday absences persist at the current rate or increase, we would consider a modest evening uptitration of levetiracetam to 1000 mg while monitoring mood and fatigue, or alternatively rationalising valproate to a more even split dosing. For now, plan is conservative monitoring given the patient’s preference. 

We will review in three months, or sooner if she experiences more than two generalised tonic–clonic seizures in any four-week period, new injury, or concerning mood change. 

Yours sincerely

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Emily Carter (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)

To: neuro.clinic@kch.nhs.uk
Cc: Dr Michael Hughes (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Priya Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Clinic review and ongoing management

Hi Emily

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Type not specified in current records


Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily
2. Clobazam 10 mg at night


Present Seizure Frequency:

Currently reporting monthly seizures, typically brief focal-onset episodes with rapid recovery as described by the family. Since commencing ketogenic diet therapy, the family notes a marked reduction in seizure frequency with only four brief seizures recorded in 2017 so far. This improvement has continued, and there have been no prolonged events or injuries this year.


Plan of Action:

At the last visit we made a minor adjustment by consolidating clobazam to night-time dosing while maintaining the lamotrigine dose. The patient and family report better sleep, improved alertness, and fewer breakthrough events, aligning with the pattern of monthly seizures only. No adverse effects have been noted from the ketogenic diet or current medications. We will:
- Continue lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily and clobazam 10 mg nocte unchanged.
- Maintain ketogenic diet therapy with ongoing dietetic support.
- Provide a rescue plan with buccal midazolam as previously prescribed for any seizure exceeding 5 minutes (not required to date).
- Monitor mood, sleep, and adherence; family to continue seizure diary and record any missed doses or intercurrent illness.
- Arrange routine bloods (U&E, LFTs, bicarbonate, lipid profile) and weight/BMI at the next nurse-led review in 3 months given the ongoing diet therapy.

The trajectory is clearly improving compared with previous years, with fewer and shorter events and stable cognition reported by school and parents. I will review again in 4 months, or sooner if the monthly seizures increase in duration, cluster, or result in injury.

With best wishes

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 09 April 2019

Dr A. Patel
Riverside Medical Practice

12 Riverbank Way
London SE1 5AB
Dear Dr A. Patel
Michael Turner, DOB: 14-03-1955, Hospital No: H937521 NHS No. 8421905630
Flat 3, 28 Willow Street, London, SE1 3JT 

Diagnoses/summary: History of recurrent unprovoked seizures of uncertain character and cause. Multiple routine EEGs previously nondiagnostic. No clear structural lesion identified on prior brain imaging per patient report.

Prior medication trials (per patient and records): Sodium valproate (sedation and tremor), carbamazepine (skin rash), levetiracetam (irritability), lamotrigine (insufficient benefit), clobazam PRN (helpful for clusters but daytime drowsiness). No history of topiramate, zonisamide, lacosamide, perampanel, or brivaracetam use.

Comorbidities: Mild hypertension (on amlodipine). No known cardiac murmur. No history of head injury or CNS infection. No family history of epilepsy recalled.

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He is a newly retired secondary-school teacher living alone. He reports a predictable daily routine with early mornings, scheduled walks, and reduced social interaction since retirement. He keeps a seizure diary on paper and on his phone. He describes episodes that remain variably stereotyped. He notes that over the course of most calendar cycles he will have several events, sometimes in loose clusters, with longer quiet spells in between. He associates poorer sleep and missed meals with increased likelihood of events. He denies tongue biting or prolonged post-event confusion in every instance, though on occasion he experiences notable fatigue afterwards. There is no clear photic trigger, and he does not drive.

Current medication:
- Amlodipine 5 mg once daily
- Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for clusters (used sparingly)
- Vitamin D 1000 IU once daily

Examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable. No focal neurological deficits. Blood pressure 138/82. He brought recent home BP readings which are broadly similar. Diary review suggests several events spread across most months, typically brief, with occasional back-to-back occurrences on successive days. No injuries reported.

Investigations and plans:
- Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D level, thyroid function.
- Arrange MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) to update prior imaging from several years ago, as records provided were incomplete.
- Discussed treatment options, including introducing a different anti-seizure medicine. He wishes to consider this after reviewing the MRI and bloods. We also discussed safety at home given that he lives alone: kettle use seated, avoiding high ladders, and considering a wearable alert device. He has already placed pans on back hobs and keeps the bathroom door unlocked.
- Agreed to continue clobazam PRN for short clusters only and to maintain a detailed seizure diary noting sleep, meals, and stressors.
- Provided information on local peer support groups; he will explore options that fit his routine to mitigate social isolation.

Follow-up:
- Telephone review by epilepsy nurse in 6–8 weeks to check diary, adherence, and side effects if any changes occur.
- Face-to-face clinic review in 3–4 months or sooner if events increase in intensity, duration, or lead to injury.
- Emergency plan discussed: seek urgent help if an event lasts longer than 5 minutes or if there are repeated events without full recovery.

Thank you for your continued care and support with blood pressure monitoring and general health maintenance. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim.

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr Patel
Riverside Health Centre

12 Riverside Way, London SE1 2AB
Dear Dr Patel
Wendy Brown, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: K482715 NHS No. 6592841037
Flat 7, Brookside Avenue, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 2QD

Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent seizures of undetermined classification; prior routine EEGs non-diagnostic; MRI brain previously non-lesional.

Previous medication: Lamotrigine (fatigue, no clear benefit), Levetiracetam (irritability), Carbamazepine (dizziness), Sodium valproate (weight gain), Lacosamide (nausea), Clobazam PRN (sedation), Phenytoin (gum changes). Not tried: Topiramate, Zonisamide, Pregabalin, Perampanel, Rufinamide, Tiagabine.

Comorbidity: History of migraine without aura; vitamin D insufficiency treated in 2023.

I reviewed Wendy Brown in clinic today, accompanied by her partner. She reports ongoing events that she describes as sudden pauses with loss of awareness followed by brief confusion; at times these are preceded by a sensation of pressure in the chest, but there is no consistent warning. She notes the events are occurring bimonthly on average, though some months she has none and then two in quick succession. She keeps a diary corroborated by her partner. There have been no tongue bites or significant injuries, and no clear triggers identified. Sleep is fragmented due to shift work; caffeine intake is moderate; alcohol minimal.

Since her last review, she tapered off Lacosamide under GP supervision because of persistent nausea. She is currently off regular antiseizure medication and prefers to avoid benzodiazepines unless absolutely necessary. She is interested in non-pharmacological strategies and asked about wearable alert devices; we discussed their role and limitations.

Examination today was unremarkable. Blood pressure 118/72, pulse 72 regular. Neurological exam normal. Review of prior investigations: MRI brain (2017) reported structurally normal; routine EEGs in 2016 and 2021 without interictal epileptiform activity. No prolonged monitoring to date. We discussed the uncertainty around the nature of her events and the value of capturing typical events on ambulatory/sleep-deprived EEG or inpatient video-EEG if needed.

Plan:
- Arrange ambulatory EEG (48–72 hours) aiming to capture typical events that occur bimonthly; if nondiagnostic and events persist, consider inpatient video-EEG monitoring.
- Blood tests: FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, magnesium, vitamin D, B12, TSH to rule out contributors to reduced threshold for events.
- Safety advice provided (first aid around seizures, bathing precautions, cooking with care, and general injury prevention). Driving discussed as per DVLA guidance for episodes of altered awareness; she reports she is currently not driving.
- Lifestyle: optimise sleep hygiene; limit caffeine to mornings; maintain hydration; continue migraine management with simple analgesia early in the attack and consider GP review for prophylaxis if frequency increases.
- Medication options explained in neutral terms, including Topiramate and Zonisamide; patient prefers to defer starting treatment until after ambulatory EEG unless event frequency increases. She will contact us urgently if there is any escalation or injury.
- Provide information on seizure first aid to partner and signpost to patient support resources.

Follow-up: Nurse-led telephone check-in in 6–8 weeks to review ambulatory EEG scheduling and interim events; clinic review in 4 months, earlier if required.

Yours sincerely

Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL

No clear triggers have been identified, though he notes poor sleep and increased stress related to his current housing situation.

Since the last community review arranged via his GP, he has continued with Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d. and Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d. He is also prescribed Clobazam 10 mg nocte as needed, which he has used on five occasions over the past three months when sleep has been particularly disrupted. He reports good adherence; he uses a pill organiser and phone reminders. He denies new neurological symptoms, tongue biting, or significant injuries. There has been no recent hospital attendance for seizures.

He is presently awaiting relocation from temporary accommodation; he reports crowded living conditions in a shared space, fragmented sleep due to noise, and difficulty maintaining regular routines. He feels this has contributed to fatigue and low mood, though he denies persistent depressive symptoms. Alcohol intake is minimal and he does not use recreational drugs. There is no recent intercurrent illness. He is not driving and understands current DVLA guidance as previously discussed.

On examination today he was well, alert and oriented. Speech, cranial nerves, limb tone, power, coordination and gait were unremarkable. No rashes or oedema. Blood pressure 126/78, pulse 72 regular. Weight stable.

We discussed management options. Given the current pattern of bimonthly seizures and the potential influence of sleep disruption in crowded accommodation, we agreed to prioritise stabilising sleep and routine while maintaining his present antiepileptic regimen. He will continue Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d., Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte p.r.n. for breakthrough sleep disturbance. I have arranged screening bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) and requested a repeat Levetiracetam level for reference. An updated EEG has been requested to reassess background activity, and we will consider ambulatory recording if events cluster.

Seizure first aid and safety at home were revisited. He would like to be contacted by the epilepsy nurse specialist for practical advice on sleep hygiene and support while he awaits rehousing; I have sent the referral today. He is aware he can contact the team if the frequency increases, if there are new features such as prolonged events, injury, or any intolerance to medication.

Plan:
- Continue Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d. and Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d.; Clobazam 10 mg nocte p.r.n. for sleep-related exacerbations.
- Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFTs; Levetiracetam level for reference.
- EEG requested; consider ambulatory recording if needed.
- Seizure diary issued; reinforce sleep hygiene and routine.
- Referral to epilepsy nurse specialist for guidance and support given crowded living conditions and disrupted sleep.
- Review in clinic in 4 months or sooner if bimonthly seizures increase in frequency or severity.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Sarah Ahmed 
Consultant Neurologist  
Centre for Epilepsy  
King’s College Hospital, London  

Dear Dr Sarah Ahmed, 

Mr Thomas Reed, DOB: 22-09-1991, Hospital No: R847362 NHS No. 1029384756  
Flat 5, 12 Brook Lane, London, SE5 9AB  

Diagnosis: 

Generalised epilepsy with bimonthly seizures despite adherence to current regimen 

Aetiology: 

Likely genetic generalised epilepsy phenotype; no structural lesion identified on MRI brain (2024) 

Other Medical Problems: 

Shift work–related circadian rhythm disruption; mild tension-type headaches; vitamin D insufficiency on replacement 

Management Plan: 

- Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte; maintain single manufacturer.  
- Introduce slow-release formulation at night to reduce early-morning breakthrough events.  
- Arrange ambulatory EEG with sleep capture given nocturnal and early-morning vulnerability.  
- Bloods in 6 weeks: FBC, LFTs, valproate trough level.  
- Letter for employer supporting mitigation of rotating shifts, particularly consecutive nights, due to established seizure provocation from circadian misalignment.  
- Safety advice reinforced: no driving; SUDEP and seizure first-aid discussed; avoid sleep deprivation and excess alcohol.  
- Review in three months via clinic; earlier if clusters or injuries occur.  

History and Current Status: 

This patient reports bimonthly seizures, generally occurring after sequences of night shifts and rapid rota changes. Events are described as sudden loss of awareness with bilateral tonic–clonic activity lasting 1–2 minutes, followed by post-ictal confusion and myalgia. No consistent aura. Witness accounts from colleagues corroborate generalised onset without focal features. He notes that sleep restriction and switching between day and night duties are the strongest triggers; alcohol is minimal and there is good medication adherence. There have been no injuries or incontinence. The last two seizures were approximately eight and sixteen weeks ago, aligning with the bimonthly pattern. 

Investigations: 

- EEG (2023): Generalised spike-and-wave discharges with photic sensitivity.  
- MRI brain (2024): Normal.  
- Bloods (May 2025): LFTs normal, valproate level within therapeutic range.  

Discussion: 

The semiology and EEG support generalised epilepsy. Persisting bimonthly seizures appear temporally linked to circadian disruption from rotating night shifts. We discussed non-pharmacological strategies to stabilise sleep timing and the clinical rationale for workplace adjustments. A switch to nocte slow-release valproate may help with early-morning vulnerability; we will reassess following ambulatory EEG and updated bloods. 

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division

From: Dr Priya Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 02 August 2024 10:15
To: epilepsy.clinic@kch.nhs.uk
Cc: Dr Michael O’Connor (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Emily Chen (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Review and medication adjustment

Dear Dr Patel,

Epilepsy diagnosis:
Combined generalised and focal epilepsy. The patient reports events consistent with both generalised seizures and focal seizures, including brief focal aware sensory auras that sometimes progress, as well as separate episodes with generalised onset.

Current medication:
1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
2. Topiramate 50 mg twice daily

Current seizure frequency:
The patient reports uncertainty when recalling counts due to clustering; they believe there were 3 or 5 seizures last month. Two were typical brief focal aware episodes with right-hand paraesthesia and preserved awareness, and one to three events were generalised with loss of awareness, a brief convulsion, and post-event myalgia lasting several hours. No clear precipitant identified beyond poor sleep in the week prior.

Assessment:
The history supports co-existing generalised and focal seizure types. There has been an apparent increase in generalised events over the last month despite good adherence and stable lamotrigine levels (patient-reported, awaiting serum confirmation). They deny intercurrent illness or new psychoactive substances. They note heightened stress at work and occasional missed meals, which may lower seizure threshold.

Plan of action:
- Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily.
- Increase topiramate to 75 mg twice daily for two weeks, then 100 mg twice daily if tolerated. Discussed potential cognitive side effects and the need for adequate hydration.
- If further generalised events occur despite this, we will consider adding valproate if not contraindicated, or brivaracetam as an alternative; final choice to be guided by tolerability and comorbidities at next review.
- Arrange MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) and routine EEG with sleep deprivation to better characterise both focal and generalised features.
- Safety advice reinforced: no driving in accordance with DVLA guidance; avoid sleep deprivation and alcohol binges; ensure supervised bathing.
- Follow-up in 3 months, sooner if further clusters occur.

With best wishes,

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr A. Patel
Consultant Neurologist,  

Samuel Green, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: KCH723518 NHS No. 9983214576  
12 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 3QH

Thank you for asking me to review this patient in our epilepsy clinic. He has a remote history of mild traumatic brain injury in his twenties without documented loss of consciousness beyond a few minutes and no neurosurgical intervention at that time. He reports that his first seizures occurred several years later and that, over time, his events have evolved with a clear focal onset. Yesterday he experienced three tonic-clonic seizures yesterday, each preceded by a stereotyped warning of a rising epigastric sensation, brief déjà vu, and impaired awareness with right-hand automatisms lasting around 30–60 seconds before secondary generalisation. His partner confirms post-ictal confusion for 20–30 minutes after each event.

On current history and semiology, this is most consistent with focal epilepsy. He describes interictal brief auras occurring approximately once or twice per week without progression, and nocturnal events are rare. Known triggers include sleep deprivation and missed meals; he denies alcohol excess. There is no family history of epilepsy. He has noted occasional word-finding difficulty for several hours after larger seizures but no persistent focal deficits.

Medication history: He is taking lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1 g twice daily with good adherence by report; no significant adverse effects beyond mild irritability on levetiracetam which he feels is manageable. He has not previously tried lacosamide or brivaracetam. No known drug allergies.

Examination today between events was unremarkable with normal cranial nerves, no lateralising motor signs, intact coordination, and normal gait. Cardiovascular and general examination were also normal.

Prior investigations: A routine EEG from 2023 was reported as showing intermittent left temporal sharp waves. Brain MRI (epilepsy protocol) from the same year described subtle left mesial temporal T2/FLAIR signal without volume loss; no acute lesions. Basic bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs) in June 2025 were within normal limits.

Plan discussed with the patient: Given the focal semiology with secondary generalisation and the recent clustering of three tonic-clonic seizures yesterday, I have recommended an urgent ambulatory EEG with sleep to capture interictal activity and to reassess localisation, along with repeat MRI using an updated temporal lobe protocol. We will also check lamotrigine and levetiracetam trough levels and standard bloods. He is keen to continue current treatment for now; we discussed potential adjustment to introduce lacosamide as add-on if further generalised seizures occur pending results. He will maintain a detailed seizure diary including auras, precipitating factors, and recovery times. Safety advice regarding driving, bathing, and machinery has been reiterated in accordance with current DVLA guidance.

I will review him in six weeks or sooner if there is any escalation. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim.

Yours sincerely

Seizure disorder with suboptimal control and troublesome treatment-related adverse effects

Undetermined despite prior routine EEG and MRI brain without a clear structural correlate

Generalised anxiety symptoms related to health, intermittent migraine without aura, vitamin D insufficiency on replacement

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Anita Bains
Riverside Medical Practice  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Anita Bains
Riverside Medical Practice,  

Liam Carter, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: KCH1029384 NHS No. 9432275619  
12 Brookfield Road, London, SE15 3HT

Thank you for referring this patient to the neurology clinic. I reviewed him today with his partner present. He reports a longstanding history of generalised epilepsy, with onset in late adolescence, previously managed in secondary care. Over the past six months he describes two drop attacks and five epileptic spasms. The drop attacks have occurred without clear warning, are brief, and have resulted in minor abrasions only; recovery has been rapid. The epileptic spasms are usually clustered in the morning shortly after waking, each lasting only a few seconds with brief trunk flexion and arm abduction, without prolonged confusion. He denies any focal onset symptoms. There is no consistent sleep deprivation or intercurrent illness preceding events. He commutes mainly by bicycle and continues his usual work as a graphic designer.

He has a past diagnosis of generalised epilepsy based on prior EEG demonstrating generalised spike–wave discharges and a normal structural MRI (2019). There is a family history of epilepsy in a maternal cousin. Current treatment is sodium valproate 1 g twice daily with good tolerability; he reports occasional mild tremor but no weight change or mood disturbance. Adherence appears reliable. He has not required emergency medication in the past year and has had no hospital admissions. There is no history of psychosis, and mood is reported as stable. He does not drink to excess and denies recreational drug use.

Neurological examination today was unremarkable. Cardiovascular and general examination were within normal limits. Routine bloods from his GP in May 2025 (FBC, U&E, LFTs, glucose, B12, folate, TFTs) were normal by report. We discussed monitoring and documentation of events. Given the recurrence profile of two drop attacks and five epileptic spasms in the past six months, and the established generalised epilepsy diagnosis, I suggested we obtain an updated routine EEG to reassess interictal activity and a serum valproate trough level to confirm therapeutic range. We also discussed possible future adjustment to therapy should spasms persist, including consideration of lamotrigine in combination, though he prefers no change today pending results. He will continue to record events on a simple calendar and bring this to the next review.

Plan agreed with the patient:
- Arrange routine EEG within 6–8 weeks.
- Check valproate trough level and LFTs via GP surgery.
- No immediate medication change; review after investigations with results to be shared.
- Provide a brief work note confirming attendance at hospital clinic today, as requested.

I will write again once results are available. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim.

Yours sincerely

Dear Dr Eleanor Wright,

Michael Turner, DOB: 15-03-1986, Hospital No: H392847 NHS No. 9034756128
22 Brookfield Avenue, Balham, London SW12 0NN

Diagnoses:

Focal epilepsy with focal impaired-awareness seizures (onset 2017)
MRI brain (2021) unremarkable; interictal EEG (2022) left temporal sharp waves

Current Medication:

Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily
Lacosamide 100 mg twice daily

Plan:

Continue current antiepileptic regimen; maintain seizure diary and reminders
Reinforce sleep hygiene and regular medication timing
Telephone review in 6 months, earlier if breakthrough events increase

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He reports a clear improvement in seizure control over the past year, which he attributes to using consistent seizure diary/reminders that have markedly improved adherence. Seizure burden has been substantially reduced following dose adjustment, with only seven focal impaired-awareness seizures reported so far this year. At present, his typical pattern is a focal seizure monthly, usually brief (1–2 minutes) with automatisms and post-event fatigue, and without generalisation.

He has not reported any medication side effects beyond transient dizziness when doses were first increased; these have settled. Sleep has been more regular, and he is avoiding missed doses using phone alarms. There have been no emergency department attendances, injuries, or prolonged events.

Given this sustained improvement and the current frequency of a focal seizure monthly, I have advised continuing levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily and lacosamide 100 mg twice daily without change. We discussed red flags (increase in seizure frequency, events clustering, or any evolution to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures) and he will contact the service promptly if these occur. He will continue his seizure diary and bring it to the next review. Driving advice remains in line with DVLA guidance for focal epilepsy; we reiterated the need to report any change that would affect eligibility.

I have arranged a telephone follow-up in six months. Please feel free to contact me if there are any concerns or if earlier review is required.

With best wishes,

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Emma Clarke (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 07 July 2024 10:15
To: kch.epilepsyclinic@nhs.net
Cc: Dr Ravi Desai (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Helen Morton (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Clinic review and medication adjustment

Hi Emma

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Primary generalised epilepsy

Present Medication:

1. Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily
2. Clobazam 10 mg at night

Present Seizure Frequency:

The patient, who has a learning disability, attends with a carer who assists with communication and maintains a seizure log. Over the past three months, the carer’s records indicate brief generalised tonic–clonic seizures occurring exclusively after nights of curtailed sleep, with no events reported when sleep has been adequate.

Plan of Action:

Given the clear temporal association with reduced sleep and otherwise stable control, we discussed optimising nocturnal coverage and minimising sedative burden during the day. We will maintain sodium valproate at the current dose and introduce a small evening top‑up of clobazam to improve resilience to sleep loss on higher‑risk nights identified by the carer.

Please adjust clobazam as follows: continue 10 mg at night on routine days; on evenings preceding anticipated short sleep (e.g. travel or early starts as identified by the carer), increase to 15 mg that night only. If morning sedation occurs, revert to 10 mg. No changes to sodium valproate at present.

We reinforced sleep hygiene measures with the carer (consistent bedtime, limiting late caffeine, keeping the sleep environment quiet) and asked them to continue detailed logging of sleep duration and seizure activity. If seizures begin to occur despite adequate sleep, we will consider transitioning clobazam to an alternative adjunct such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam, balancing tolerability and interaction profile with valproate.

I have arranged follow‑up in four months, sooner if events increase or safety concerns arise. The carer has our clinic contact details for interim advice.

With best wishes

Dear Dr Eleanor Patel,

John Smith, DOB: 11-07-1984, Hospital No: S845921 NHS No. 7823495610
34 Kensington Road, London, W8 5NP

Diagnoses:

Primary generalised epilepsy with prior generalised tonic–clonic seizures (first in 2006, relapse August 2018). EEG (October 2018) demonstrated generalised spike-and-wave activity consistent with generalised epilepsy.

Lamotrigine 75 mg bd

He remains on Lamotrigine 75 mg twice daily, taken consistently. He has noticed no rash or systemic side effects, though he reports occasional dizziness on waking.

I have arranged blood tests including routine safety monitoring and trough lamotrigine level, and I will reassess the results to guide any future medication adjustment. We also discussed DVLA guidance; he is currently driving, and I reiterated that any further generalised events or impaired awareness episodes while driving would require cessation and notification in line with regulations.

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 16 February 2016 

Dr Eleanor Patel
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Eleanor Patel
Consultant Neurologist,  

Sophie Bennett, DOB: 14-03-1993, Hospital No: KCH728519 NHS No. 9076143258  
12 Celandine Court, Dulwich, London SE21 8JT

Thank you for your referral and for the accompanying details. I reviewed Sophie Bennett in clinic today following recent postpartum changes. She reports a clear deterioration over the past two months, with increasing fatigue, low mood, and a subjective sense that her seizures are clustering more often. She is breastfeeding and sleeping in fragmented blocks, which she feels has amplified both her tiredness and seizure burden. Her partner corroborates a noticeable decline in resilience and longer post-event recovery times.

She has a known diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy. On history, there are two distinct event types:  
- Generalised episodes: abrupt loss of awareness with bilateral tonic-clonic activity, preceded at times by a brief “whole-head pressure” sensation. Post-ictal confusion typically lasts 30–60 minutes.  
- Focal episodes: focal aware onset with a rising epigastric sensation, right-hand clenching, and brief speech arrest lasting 30–90 seconds, occasionally progressing to impaired awareness.

She additionally describes light-triggered attacks: in busy retail settings and when scrolling rapidly through high-contrast digital content, she experiences brief shimmering in the visual field, eyelid flutter, and then an escalation to her usual generalised convulsions if exposure continues. These light-provoked events have increased from approximately once monthly before delivery to occurring every one to two weeks postpartum. In the past four weeks she reports three nocturnal convulsions and six focal aware events, which is a significant increase from her late antenatal baseline.

Medication history: currently on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1 g twice daily. She was stable antenatally on the same regimen but had better sleep and fewer triggers. No recent missed doses reported; however, she notes occasional delays with evening doses due to infant care demands. No new intercurrent illness, alcohol intake minimal, and no recreational drugs. She has not resumed driving and remains compliant with DVLA advice.

Examination today was unremarkable neurologically. Mental state suggested low mood and tearfulness, without psychotic features. There were no focal deficits on examination. Bloods available from the GP last month showed normal U&Es and LFTs; antiseizure medication levels were not checked.

Impression: combined generalised and focal epilepsy with postpartum deterioration in seizure control, plausibly exacerbated by sleep deprivation, physiological postpartum changes, and possible heightened photosensitivity manifesting as light-provoked attacks. Her overall condition is deteriorating compared with the pre-delivery baseline, with increased frequency of both focal and generalised events and longer recovery.

Plan:  
1. Arrange urgent serum lamotrigine and levetiracetam trough levels to guide dose optimisation.  
2. Bring forward EEG with photic stimulation and sleep deprivation protocol to characterise the light-provoked component and interictal burden.  
3. Expedite MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) if not updated within the last two years.  
4. Sleep hygiene and practical postpartum adjustments discussed; she will trial scheduled rest periods supported by her partner for consistent medication timing.  
5. Provide written guidance on reducing light-trigger exposure (screen brightness adjustments, flicker-reduction settings, and protective eyewear in high-contrast environments).  
6. Safety counselling reiterated regarding bathing, infant handling when drowsy or post-ictal, and seizure first aid.  
7. Liaise with perinatal mental health for assessment of postpartum low mood, as this may be contributing to perceived worsening and coping.  
8. Review in six weeks, sooner if further clusters or injuries occur. She was given the urgent advice line and instructed to seek emergency assessment for prolonged seizures or repeated events without recovery.

Thank you for your continued care. I will update you following investigations and once serum levels are available.

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 02 October 2025

Dr A Patel
Riverside Health Centre

12 Brook Lane

Southwark
London SE1 0AB
Dear Dr A Patel
Jordan Ellis, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: H739205 NHS No. 8421906753
Flat 3, 28 Willow Court, London, SE15 4JG 

Diagnoses/summary: Recurrent seizures with uncertain classification; prior EEGs non-diagnostic and one ambulatory study reported sporadic non-specific changes. No clearly identified precipitant other than sudden environmental sounds reported by the patient and family. 

MRI brain 2019 reported structurally unremarkable appearances; no focal lesion detected.

Previous medication: Levetiracetam (behavioural irritability, seizures persisted), Sodium valproate (weight gain and tremor), Carbamazepine (dizziness, hyponatraemia), Lamotrigine (partial benefit but ongoing events), Clobazam PRN (some reduction in clusters), Lacosamide (no clear benefit), Topiramate (word-finding difficulty), Zonisamide (appetite suppression and insomnia).

Not taken: Perampanel, Brivaracetam, Rufinamide, Oxcarbazepine, Cenobamate, Pregabalin, Tiagabine.

Comorbidities: Migraine without aura; mild asthma. No known cardiac disease; echocardiogram 2021 normal. 

I reviewed Jordan Ellis in clinic today, accompanied by their partner. They described daily brief events and approximately 2–3 longer episodes per month. Of note, they and their partner have observed that abrupt, unexpected noises (for example, a dropped plate or sudden door slam) often precede the shorter events; these are described as a rapid startle followed by a freeze and loss of awareness for up to 30–60 seconds with occasional right-hand fumbling, then a short period of confusion. There is no consistent nocturnal pattern. They report no sustained aura. Injuries have been limited to minor bruises.

They continue to work part-time in an office role and are not driving. Mood has been variable but there is no current self-harm risk. Sleep is reported as fragmented. Alcohol intake minimal; no recreational drugs. Family history non-contributory.

Current medication:
- Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
- Clobazam 10 mg at night (with 5 mg as needed for clusters, used approximately once weekly)
- Salbutamol inhaler PRN
- Magnesium supplement (patient-initiated)

Plan:
- We discussed options including a cautious switch from lamotrigine to brivaracetam, or trial of perampanel, acknowledging prior behavioural effects on levetiracetam. The patient wishes to consider brivaracetam first; I provided written information and asked them to contact the epilepsy nurse specialist (ENS) within 2 weeks to confirm preference.
- Safety advice reinforced, particularly around baths vs showers, kitchen hazards, and using a soft alarm tone where feasible given the tendency of abrupt noise to precede brief events.
- Seizure diary to continue, with particular note of context, sound environment, and time-of-day. Partner will attempt to capture a safe video of typical episodes on their phone for review.
- Request repeat routine EEG with additional sound-related activation procedures if tolerated, and consider ambulatory EEG if routine study remains uninformative.
- Bloods: U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D, lamotrigine level for reference.
- Referral to ENS for telephone follow-up in 4–6 weeks to review frequency, tolerability, and to finalise medication strategy.
- Driving: patient not driving; current guidance reiterated.

I will review Jordan Ellis in clinic in approximately 4 months, sooner if there is any deterioration or if they elect to commence a new antiseizure medication requiring closer titration.

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Ahmed  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Sophie Turner, DOB: 12-04-1991, Hospital No: H482930 NHS No. 9038475621  
19 Garden Mews, London, W2 6PL 

Medication: 

Sodium valproate 500 mg in the morning and 1000 mg at night. Tolerated without notable adverse effects; no reported weight change, gastrointestinal upset, or tremor. Folic acid 5 mg once daily (patient-led prior to planned conception discussion). 

Thank you for reviewing this patient who has a diagnosis of generalised epilepsy. Since our last appointment, she describes episodes that her partner mainly witnesses during the night; however, he was not present at today’s review, so collateral details are second-hand. She reports feeling unrefreshed on waking on approximately two mornings per week and occasional tongue soreness, with bedclothes found disordered. There have been no definite daytime convulsions. Daytime alertness is generally satisfactory, though she notes transient fogginess after poorer nights. No injuries, incontinence, or prolonged postictal confusion have been recorded. 

Regarding seizure pattern, she describes what she calls “exercise-associated spillover days,” where more vigorous evening workouts are followed by a night with increased events as judged by her morning symptoms and smartwatch movement alerts. I explained that, in the context of generalised epilepsy, exertion later in the day may lower seizure threshold indirectly through sleep disruption and dehydration rather than being a direct trigger. She will try shifting strenuous activity earlier and maintaining hydration and a consistent sleep schedule. 

Examination today is normal. There are no focal neurological signs. Bloods from last month (U&E, LFT, FBC) were within reference range. A prior EEG showed generalised spike–wave discharges with photic sensitivity; MRI brain (2019) was unremarkable. 

Plan: 
- Continue sodium valproate 500 mg AM and 1000 mg PM. As the events are predominantly nocturnal and currently without daytime impairment, we will not alter the dose today. 
- If nocturnal episodes persist at a similar frequency over the next 6–8 weeks despite sleep and exercise timing adjustments, we will consider either a modest nocturnal valproate increase or switch to an alternative broad-spectrum agent after discussion. 
- Safety: advised on night-time precautions (low bed height, clear floor space), and to avoid sleep deprivation. She does not drive. 
- Reproductive counselling provided today; if pregnancy is anticipated, we will review alternatives to valproate and shared decision-making will be undertaken promptly. 

We will review her again in four months, sooner if daytime events emerge or if there are any injuries or prolonged episodes. 

Yours sincerely

Dear Dr Aisha Rahman,

Re: Michael Turner, DOB: 14-03-1987, Hospital No: L392847, NHS No: 9045173821
12 Fernbank Close, Wimbledon, London SW19 3PL

Diagnoses:

Recurrent seizure episodes of uncertain classification. EEG pending review.

Current Medication:

Lamotrigine 75 mg twice daily

Plan:

- Continue lamotrigine 75 mg twice daily without interruption
- Arrange urgent sleep-deprived EEG and repeat serum lamotrigine level
- Safety counselling regarding sleep hygiene, jet lag management, and high-risk activities

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today following a period of clinical decline. Since undertaking recent long-haul travel across several time zones, he reports marked circadian disruption with difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep. Over the past six weeks he describes three witnessed convulsive episodes and several brief staring events with loss of awareness. Of note, he identifies a pattern of episodes clustering after intake of strong coffee and energy drinks during periods of sleep loss; he refers to these as "stimulant-linked attacks" occurring roughly once every one to two weeks since the travel. Given the recent escalation in frequency and the emergence of events despite ongoing lamotrigine, I have advised strict adherence to regular sleep and avoidance of identified stimulants. We will check his lamotrigine level and consider dose optimisation once results are available. I have also arranged a sleep-deprived EEG to assess for any interictal abnormalities. He has been provided with written safety advice, including not driving and avoiding operating machinery until seizure control is re-established.

I will review him by telephone in four weeks to assess interim stability and blood results, with a scheduled in-person appointment at three months. He and his family are aware to contact us urgently should there be any further convulsive events or injuries.

With best wishes,

Yours sincerely,

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 14 September 2025 

Dr Amelia Rhodes
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Amelia Rhodes
Consultant Neurologist,  

Daniel Walker, DOB: 14-03-1989, Hospital No: KCH928374 NHS No. 9475123068  
12 Fernbrook Gardens, London, SE24 8QJ

Thank you for referring this patient for neurological review. I met him today in clinic accompanied by his partner. He described longstanding episodes that he and his family have termed “spells,” beginning in his late teens. The events are stereotyped: he experiences a brief warning of a rising internal tension and a sense of detachment, followed by behavioural arrest with fixed gaze and lip chewing reported by witnesses. On some occasions there is right arm stiffening and a brief cry. He is typically confused for 15–30 minutes afterwards and complains of a throbbing headache with pronounced fatigue.

Regarding periodicity, he and his partner report that the events tend to group together over several days in a repeating pattern roughly every four to five weeks. Within these burst periods the number of episodes varies and has not been reliably logged; outside these periods he may go a week or two without events. This “regular bursts every few weeks; number during bursts not well documented” pattern has been their usual experience for years. He started levetiracetam six months ago after trials of lamotrigine and carbamazepine were discontinued for rash and dizziness respectively. Notably, since commencing current therapy the overall pattern has persisted without clear change in frequency or recovery time.

There is no consistent relationship with sleep deprivation or alcohol, though he suspects that high work stress and missed meals may act as triggers. No tongue laceration or incontinence has been witnessed. He has had two emergency attendances in the last year for cluster days with prolonged confusion; bloods at those times were unremarkable and a CT head performed three years ago was reported normal. He has never had status epilepticus or significant injury from these events. Family history is non-contributory. He does not drive and is aware of DVLA guidance as previously discussed with his GP.

On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal speech, cranial nerves intact, no focal motor deficit, and normal coordination and gait. Cardiovascular and general examination were unremarkable. There were no features of ongoing post-event confusion at the time of review. Blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm regular.

We discussed next steps. The main issue at present is to clarify the nature of the events and obtain objective correlation. He is agreeable to an ambulatory EEG with event diary, followed by consideration of inpatient video-EEG if the ambulatory study does not capture typical episodes. I have also recommended structured documentation using a calendar or smartphone app to record the timing of warning symptoms, event duration, and recovery features, so that we can quantify numbers during the clustered periods. He will continue levetiracetam at his current dose as he reports tolerability but no perceived benefit so far; we will not change treatment until we have more diagnostic information. I have requested routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D) to be done at his GP surgery for baseline monitoring.

For safety, we reinforced standard advice around adequate sleep, regular meals, moderated alcohol intake, and seeking urgent help if any event lasts more than five minutes, occurs back-to-back without recovery, or if he sustains significant injury. He understands not to swim unsupervised, to avoid heights, and to take showers instead of baths.

I will review him in clinic after the ambulatory EEG. Thank you again for the referral and for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there is any additional history or prior imaging that would be helpful to obtain before telemetry.

Yours sincerely

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today following three months of intermittent brief events. They describe stereotyped episodes with a sudden sense of "switching off" and loss of awareness for 10–20 seconds, sometimes followed by a short period of confusion. There are no consistent focal auras reported. Injuries have not occurred. Family have witnessed two events and noted blank staring with unresponsiveness, without clear limb jerking. 

Regarding frequency, the patient reports that episodes tend to come in small runs: typically around four to six short spells grouped together on days when they occur, most commonly later in the day towards the evening period. There may then be several days without events. Sleep disruption and higher anxiety levels appear to precede these clusters, and caffeine excess may contribute. Alcohol intake is modest and there is no recreational drug use. 

Past medical history is notable for longstanding anxiety with intermittent low mood, currently improved on Sertraline 50 mg daily for the past six months, with no reported side effects. Screening today suggests stable mood; no suicidal ideation. They are open to psychological therapies and will discuss an IAPT referral with you. 

On examination today, neurological assessment was unremarkable. Routine blood tests earlier this year were normal. We have arranged updated baseline bloods today. An MRI brain with epilepsy protocol has been requested, and a routine EEG has been scheduled; should events remain poorly captured, we would consider ambulatory monitoring. 

Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily was started by the emergency department six weeks ago after two clusters within a fortnight. Since initiation, the patient reports a reduction in event severity and number per cluster, with no new adverse effects beyond mild initial fatigue which has settled. We discussed adherence, common triggers, and the importance of sleep regularity. A seizure diary was provided to document timing (particularly evening tendency), precipitants, and recovery features to better guide further management. 

We reviewed DVLA guidance and driving restrictions; the patient understands current requirements and will inform the DVLA as appropriate. 

I will see Emily Carter again in approximately four months to review the imaging, EEG results, and diary data. Please feel free to contact me sooner if there is any clinical concern, a significant increase in clusters, or medication intolerance. 

With best wishes,

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 23 March 2017 

Dr Patel

Dear Dr Patel,  

Sophie Williams, DOB: 14-07-1997, Hospital No: A927451 NHS No. 7482019365  
12 Riverside Close, London, SW18 2AB  

Diagnoses: 

- Generalised epilepsy.  
- History of migraine (not currently the clinical focus). 

Thank you for reviewing Sophie Williams in our epilepsy clinic. She attended today with her mother. She reports that her migraine symptoms have been stable over the past year without requiring specific prophylaxis; however, our current focus remains her epilepsy management. She confirms that her last seizure on 20/Dec occurred in the early morning with a brief generalised convulsion lasting approximately 90 seconds, followed by typical post-ictal confusion for 15–20 minutes. There have been no seizures since then, and she has had no injuries or emergency department attendances. 

Medication: She remains on sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily with good adherence; no adverse effects reported aside from mild intermittent tremor which she does not find troublesome. She has not required any rescue medication in the past six months. No other antiepileptic drugs are currently prescribed. 

Seizure control and triggers: She notes improved sleep hygiene since January and has reduced late-night screen use. There is no clear photic sensitivity. Alcohol intake is minimal. Menses remain regular without clear catamenial pattern. Family report normal cognition and mood, and she is attending college full-time. 

Examination: Pulse 74 bpm regular; BP 112/68; weight 63 kg. Neurological examination was unremarkable with no focal deficits. 

Investigations: Last EEG (May 2016) showed generalised spike–wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy. MRI brain (2015) was normal. Routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC) from February 2017 were within normal limits. 

Plan: 
- Continue sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily unchanged. 
- Reinforce adherence and ongoing sleep hygiene, given apparent benefit. 
- Safety advice reviewed, including supervision near water and avoidance of heights when alone. 
- No indication for VNS or medication change at present given stability since the last seizure on 20/Dec. 
- We will review in six months, or sooner if further seizures occur, adverse effects develop, or there are concerns regarding pregnancy planning. 

I trust this is helpful. Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require further information. 

Yours sincerely

Clinic Date: 04 November 2015

Dr A. Patel
Eastborough Neurology Centre
Neurology Outpatients, 12 Millbank Way, Eastborough EB2 4HT

Dear Dr A. Patel,

Emily Carter, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: E927451 NHS No. 6045812379
Flat 2, 16 Rowan Close, Eastborough EB3 1QP

Diagnoses:

Adult-onset seizure disorder; history of childhood febrile seizures noted.

Current Medication:

- Levetiracetam 1 g bd
- Clobazam 10 mg nocte (intermittent use for clusters)

Plan:

- Continue current antiseizure regimen without changes today while we complete further evaluation.
- Arrange prolonged ambulatory EEG and MRI brain with epilepsy protocol to clarify seizure onset and aid risk stratification.
- Provide seizure first-aid and nocturnal supervision advice; reinforce SUDEP risk discussion given ongoing nocturnal events.
- Safety counselling: bathing supervision, avoid heights/open water; driving not permitted and DVLA guidance reviewed.
- Follow-up in 3 months, sooner if escalation occurs; consider medication optimisation or addition depending on results and tolerability.

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today with her partner present. She reports a long-standing history of childhood febrile seizures, with no clear events through adolescence. In adulthood she developed recurrent seizures. Seizure control is inconsistent and while the caregiver perceives stability, she continues to have nightly generalised tonic-clonic seizures and intermittent tonic seizures 2 - 3 times per year, this has been her enduring seizure profile for many years. She describes the nocturnal events as occurring during sleep with a bitten tongue on several occasions and morning headache and myalgia. Daytime events are rare. There are no clear catamenial patterns. She identifies sleep deprivation and intercurrent illness as potential precipitants.

She is adherent with her current medication. Previous trials of lamotrigine were discontinued due to rash; topiramate caused cognitive side effects. No recent injuries, but there have been two prior bed falls without major harm. There is no family history of adult seizures. Neurological examination today is unremarkable. Routine blood tests earlier this month were within reference limits.

We discussed lifestyle measures, nocturnal safeguards (monitoring device, side-lying positioning), and the importance of regular sleep. An updated seizure diary was provided. I will review her after investigations to consider adjustments such as clobazam regularisation at night or alternative adjuncts depending on tolerability and findings.

With best wishes,

Yours sincerely

Hi Priya

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Not specified in records; classification not documented pending further correlation with history and investigations.

1. Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily (patient-reported adherence) 
2. Clobazam 10 mg at night (intermittent use as per caregiver; variable supply due to pharmacy access)

Present Seizure Frequency:

Seizure control is inconsistent and while the caregiver perceives stability, she continues to have nightly generalised tonic-clonic seizures and intermittent tonic seizures three times per year, this has been her enduring seizure profile for many years.

Relevant History and Context:

The patient resides on a houseboat/mobile home with her partner as primary caregiver. They report occasional power outages affecting the charging of phone and medical devices (including seizure alarm and medication reminder). History is patient-reported, and there are no recent emergency department records available for corroboration. She reports good tolerance of lamotrigine without rash, mood change, or balance problems. Sleep is fragmented due to nocturnal events. No clear catamenial pattern noted. Alcohol intake minimal; no recreational drugs. Medication storage sometimes impacted by damp and temperature fluctuation on the boat, as reported by the caregiver.

- No recent ASM serum levels available.

With best wishes,

Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Helen Carter (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 11 December 2014 10:15
To: neuro.epilepsyclinic@nhs.net
Cc: Dr Ravi Desai (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Emily Shaw (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Clinical update and workplace-trigger concern

Hi Helen

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Primary generalised epilepsy. The patient has a history consistent with generalised epilepsy and reports recent worsening of events in the context of environmental triggers.

Present Medication:

1. Sodium Valproate 500 mg in the morning and 1,000 mg at night
2. Clobazam 10 mg at night as required for clusters (patient-led use, typically avoided on work days due to sedation)

Present Seizure Frequency:

She told me that since her last clinic appointment she has had several myoclonic jerks, the last reported on 10-Oct. She could not quantify the total number of events and feels they are occurring more often at work compared to home.

Clinical Summary and Deterioration:

The patient describes a clear deterioration over recent weeks coinciding with a move to a new workplace where lighting is notably bright with intermittent flicker (e.g. display walls and LED panels). She reports more frequent brief morning myoclonic jerks and occasional startle-like arm twitches during late afternoon meetings under these lights. No clear sleep deprivation or missed doses were identified. There have been no known generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported, but she remains concerned about escalating myoclonic activity in this environment.

Plan of Action:

- We discussed that strong and flickering lights can exacerbate seizures in photosensitive generalised epilepsies. She will liaise with her employer’s occupational health to review lighting (e.g. use of diffusers, stable non-flicker settings) and consider screen filters and regular screen breaks.
- She will continue to maintain a detailed event and trigger diary, noting time, setting, light exposure, and any missed medication.
- No immediate medication changes were made today as she wishes to trial environmental adjustments first; we agreed this is reasonable. If events persist or escalate despite mitigation, we will consider medication optimisation at the next review.
- She was advised on safety at work and during commuting if jerks cluster.
- Follow-up arranged in eight weeks, sooner if there is any further deterioration.

With best wishes

This pattern is corroborated by diary entries and partner observation and is consistent with peer notes taken during two observed days earlier this summer. We also discussed general measures: consistent sleep routine, hydration, and pacing on high-demand days; she will continue these self-management strategies.

I will update you once monitoring is complete and we have a clearer synthesis. Please let me know if there are interim concerns or if new information arises from your records.

Yours sincerely

Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Patel  
St Thomas' Hospital  
Neurosciences Department, Westminster Bridge Road, London SE1 7EH  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Emily Dawson, DOB: 14-11-1990, Hospital No: R928417 NHS No. 7401563928  
58 Alder Grove, London, SW8 1JP  

Diagnoses: 

Symptomatic generalised epilepsy. 

I reviewed Emily Dawson in clinic today. She attends alone and reports a notable deterioration in her seizure control over the past 4–5 months. Historically, she has generalised epilepsy and she has a past history of atonic seizures, drop attacks and generalised tonic–clonic seizures one to two times per year, but seizure control has been excellent, and she has now been seizure free for several years. However, since increasing work pressures and longer hours, she has experienced clusters of jumps almost daily, particularly on workdays, consistent with her report that high workload has been a precipitating factor. She describes these as brief, sudden axial and upper limb jerks with occasional object dropping; she also notes intermittent disequilibrium and near‑falls. There have been two definite drop events in the last six weeks. No generalised tonic–clonic seizures have been witnessed, but her partner reports brief staring and word‑finding pauses on two occasions. 

She links the worsening to work‑related stress and poor sleep. Events tend to cluster on workdays per patient report, with relative improvement on weekends. There is no recent intercurrent illness, alcohol excess, or new medications. She denies missed anti‑seizure medication, though acknowledges variable timing on late shifts. Menses regular; no pregnancy. 

Current treatment: lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily; levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. She has tolerated these without rash or mood lability; mild irritability attributed to work fatigue. She is not using rescue medication currently. No vagus nerve stimulator in situ. 

Examination today was unremarkable: alert, oriented, speech fluent; cranial nerves intact; no focal motor deficit; gait steady in clinic though she describes occasional morning unsteadiness. Blood pressure 118/72, pulse 72 regular. 

Given the deterioration and daily clustering of myoclonic‑type events, I have discussed seizure safety at work (avoidance of ladders, hot surfaces; shower rather than bath; supervision with heavy machinery) and driving regulations. She does not currently drive. We agreed to obtain updated bloods (U&Es, LFTs, FBC, vitamin D) and anti‑seizure medication levels where available, and to arrange an EEG, including activation procedures, to look for generalised spike‑wave or polyspike‑wave activity. A brain MRI from 2018 was normal; we will repeat MRI if clinically indicated after EEG review. 

She will start a structured sleep routine and stress‑reduction plan (patient‑led), and keep a seizure diary noting triggers, timing, and any clusters. We also discussed the option of dose optimisation if events persist; plan to consider a cautious lamotrigine uptitration or adjunctive valproate discussion if appropriate and acceptable in future. She understands this is an interim plan while we complete investigations. 

In summary, despite several years of excellent control, there is clear worsening temporally associated with occupational stress: she has experienced clusters of jumps almost daily, with occasional drops and brief absences suggested. This represents a deterioration from her prior baseline of rare events. I have asked her to contact the service urgently if she has any generalised tonic–clonic seizures, injuries, or any prolonged clusters. 

Follow‑up in 6–8 weeks after EEG, or sooner if needed. 

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Ahmed  
Riverside Medical Centre  
12 Kingfisher Way, Hammersmith, London W6 8QZ  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Sophie Bennett, DOB: 14-05-1991, Hospital No: H438920 NHS No. 9056723411  
Flat 3, 29 Brook Street, London W1K 4DR 

Medication: 

- Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily.
- Vitamin D3 1000 IU daily.

Thank you for your ongoing care of Sophie Bennett, who attended today accompanied by her partner. We also reviewed recent employer occupational health summaries, which have been helpful collateral sources corroborating events observed in the workplace.

Current concerns: 

- Drop attacks are now reported 5 times weekly, having previously occurred only sporadically, once every few months. These have been witnessed both at home and at work, typically without warning, and recovery is rapid but followed by fatigue and mild headache. No clear precipitant has been identified, although stress and shift pattern changes were noted by the patient. Occupational health notes describe brief unresponsiveness in two events, without clear convulsive features.
- Occasional morning fogginess since the levetiracetam dose increase six months ago; no mood change reported by patient or noted by occupational health.
- No recent injuries, though one near-fall was documented by the employer’s first aider; patient now uses a soft knee support as a precaution.

Examination today was unremarkable. Cardiovascular and neurological screening were normal. Orthostatic blood pressure did not suggest postural hypotension. There were no focal deficits.

Investigations and collateral information: 

- Occupational health reports from July and September confirm multiple witnessed collapses consistent with the patient’s description. 
- Prior EEG (2023) and MRI (2022) reports were reviewed; no new imaging since. 
- We have asked the patient to provide brief smartphone video documentation from witnesses when safe and appropriate.

Plan: 

- Continue levetiracetam 1 g twice daily for now. We discussed potential adjustments, but agreed to collate additional event data first, given the recent change in frequency and the need to clarify semiology and triggers. 
- Issue a safety plan for workplace and home (avoiding heights, hot surfaces, lone working on ladders; employer already implementing reasonable adjustments per occupational health). 
- Arrange ambulatory ECG and bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D) to exclude mimics and monitor general health. 
- Book ambulatory EEG to capture typical events if feasible. 
- Provide a seizure diary template; the patient will log timing, context, sleep, stress, and menses. Occupational health will submit monthly summaries directly to clinic with patient consent.
- Driving: patient confirms she is not currently driving; we reiterated DVLA guidance as discussed previously.

Follow-up: 

- Review in 8–10 weeks, sooner if events escalate or injuries occur. We will contact you with interim results if they prompt earlier action.

Many thanks for your assistance, and please let us know if you would like us to share the workplace safety plan template for your records.

Yours sincerely

typed_input.note_text:
Epilepsy Centre

Neurosciences Division


From: Dr Emily Carter (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Sent: 13 June 2025 10:20
To: kch-epilepsy@nhs.net
Cc: Dr Ravi Desai (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Hannah O’Neill (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST)
Subject: Post-partum deterioration and treatment adjustment

Hi Emily

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Focal epilepsy, probable temporal lobe onset, with secondary generalisation reported on two occasions historically. Patient has focal epilepsy.

Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
2. Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily

Present Seizure Frequency:

Since delivery six months ago, the patient reports a perceived worsening of seizures alongside low mood and marked fatigue. In Mar she had five seizures during sleep and 5 while awake. In May she had no in sleep and one while awake. Her partner corroborates that nocturnal events in March included automatisms and post-ictal confusion on waking, while the daytime events were brief focal impaired-awareness episodes with lip smacking and speech arrest, one progressing to a bilateral tonic–clonic seizure.

Plan of Action:

The clinical picture suggests post-partum deterioration, likely influenced by sleep deprivation and mood symptoms. Despite therapeutic lamotrigine levels checked last month, breakthrough focal seizures persist. To address this:
- Increase lamotrigine to 200 mg twice daily over two weeks (increase by 25–50 mg per dose every 5–7 days as tolerated), monitoring for rash or dizziness.
- Continue levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily unchanged for now. The patient reports irritability and low mood post-partum; we discussed that levetiracetam can exacerbate mood symptoms. If mood remains problematic after lamotrigine optimisation, we will consider tapering levetiracetam and switching to brivaracetam.
- Safety: reinforce seizure first aid, no driving as per DVLA guidance following recent events, and avoid unsupervised bathing/co-sleeping with the infant.
- Support: referral to perinatal mental health team for assessment of low mood and fatigue; advise sleep hygiene strategies and partner-supported night feeds where possible.
- Investigations: arrange repeat EEG with sleep deprivation and an updated MRI epilepsy protocol (last imaging 2019). Check lamotrigine trough level in four weeks after dose escalation.
- Follow-up: review in clinic in 8–10 weeks. Earlier review if seizure frequency increases, adverse effects occur, or mood deteriorates further.

Overall, the condition is currently deteriorating in the post-partum period by patient and partner report, though May shows partial improvement; we will prioritise seizure control while addressing mood and sleep contributors.

With best wishes
